description: Software developer and founder of NG Development (since 2020). CS graduate building full-stack and mobile apps with Flutter, Laravel, MySQL and REST APIs. Creator of Life, an on-device screen-time app with an AI agent. Working solo on astronaut health monitoring: an offline-first crew app that detects health trends without Earth’s help, since Mars messages can take 24 min, plus a ground dashboard. Decision support, not diagnosis. Interests: mobile dev, health tech, space.
summary:
SkyShift is a public web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx survey into a flipbook of how any patch of sky changes over time. Enter coordinates, pick a test target, or drag the sky map, and SkyShift collects every SPHEREx exposure of that spot from NASA/IPAC IRSA, aligns them north-up on one brightness scale and plays the sky passes like a short video, with colour, single-band, difference ("what changed") and per-exposure views, Gaia and WISE overlays, contamination flags and shareable URLs.

It also uses data everyone else discards. Three in four SPHEREx images are crossed by a satellite, and the pipeline masks those pixels. SPHEREx records every streak in two cameras at the same instant, one in reflected light and one in heat. Measuring the unflagged edges of the streak, we took a satellite's temperature (279 K), identified it from SPHEREx's own position (a 1986 rocket stage, 987 km away) and estimated its size with no albedo guess. We then measured 31 trails from NASA Ames's catalogue, which their paper called unmeasurable.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SkyShift answers the challenge directly: type a right ascension and declination (or pick a target, a city, or drag the sky map and click "Load SPHEREx images here") and it shows that patch of sky as a series of SPHEREx images played like a little video, so moving and changing objects stand out.

- Every SPHEREx exposure covering the position is found through NASA/IPAC IRSA (SIA2 + cutout services, Quick Release 3 and DR1), reprojected to one north-up grid and grouped into six-monthly sky passes.

- All images of a band share one brightness scale, so a change you see is real.

- Views: false colour (4.7 / 2 / 0.9 µm), single band stacked per detector for signal-to-noise, "What changed" (later pass minus earlier: a moving star becomes a blue–amber pair), and every individual exposure with its contamination flags.

- Choice of field of view; the URL reproduces the exact view (?ra=…&dec=…&fov=…) so it can be embedded or shared.

- Sky map (Aladin Lite) with the AllWISE map, SPHEREx's own all-sky map in all 102 wavelengths with a wavelength slider, and a Gaia DR3 overlay.

- The five test targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) open instantly; new positions are fetched live, so the tool updates with each new data release.

WHAT IS NEW: THE PIXELS EVERYONE DELETES

NASA Ames found satellite trails in 73% of SPHEREx exposures (Borlaff et al. 2026). The pipeline flags them and science masks them out. SPHEREx splits light into two cameras with a dichroic mirror, so every streak is recorded twice at the same instant: in reflected sunlight (short-wave camera) and in heat (long-wave camera).

- We measure the light at the unflagged edges of the streak in both cameras and calibrate it on stars stacked from the same frame. Stars give a long/short ratio of 0.25×; our showcase streak gives 58×: not a star, and not just sunlight.

- A blackbody fit to the 4.4–5.0 µm slope gives 279 K (268–292 K).

- SPHEREx writes its own position into every file. Propagating the public satellite catalogue (SGP4) across the 115-second exposure, exactly one orbit lies on the streak: an H-1 rocket stage launched in 1986 (NORAD 16910), 987 km from the telescope.

- Heat, temperature and distance give a thermal cross-section with no guess about reflectivity (the blind spot of optical debris tracking): about 84 m², against 26 m² for the real stage side-on. Same order of magnitude; we present it as a factor-of-few check.

- A second object, COSMOS 1980, measured at 294 K, 226 km away.

- Pilot census: from NASA Ames's catalogue of 2,182 trails, whose paper states trail brightness is not measurable from Level 2 frames, we drew 107 at random (no hand-picking) and ran the same method. 31 were detected in the heat camera, every one far from the stars (median 12× vs 0.25×), and 14 glow in heat alone with no reflected light detected. To our knowledge these are the first 2–5 µm thermal colours of satellites from a public all-sky survey (earlier space-based work: MSX, 6–28 µm, 2008; WISE, geostationary objects only).

IMPACT

Space safety gets a size from heat without the reflectivity guess. Astronomers get a handle on what the streak mask leaves behind in their images. And anyone can replay a patch of sky, watch a star move, and learn what crossed it.

LIMITS (stated on the site)

Sizes are good to a factor of 2–3; temperatures need the 3.8–5 µm cameras and enough edge light; naming needs orbit data for each date. Next: name every census trail and test whether the 14 heat-only objects were in Earth's shadow.

TOOLS

Python 3.11 (FastAPI, Astropy, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, sgp4, Pillow), JavaScript/HTML/CSS, Aladin Lite v3. Frontend and backend run on cPanel hosting; long jobs run in the background so the page never times out.

Code (open source, MIT): https://github.com/ayoubna99/spherex-skyshift
